explanation:
### The bug

One line, in `write`:

```cpp
buf[(start + n) % cap] = v;
if (n < cap) { ++n; }          // and nothing else happens when n == cap
```

The slot it writes to is right in both cases. When the recorder is not full, `(start + n) % cap` is the first free slot. When it **is** full, `n == cap`, so `(start + n) % cap` is `(start + cap) % cap`, which is `start` — the oldest slot, which is exactly the one to reuse.

What it forgets is that reusing that slot *changes which value is the oldest*. The value that used to live at `start` has just been overwritten; the oldest surviving value is the one at `start + 1`. Nothing moves `start`, so `dump` keeps reading from a slot that now holds the newest value.

That is why it prints `4 2 3`: the 4 is sitting in slot 0 where the 1 was, and `dump` still believes slot 0 is the beginning.

### The fix

```cpp
buf[(start + n) % cap] = v;
if (n == cap) { start = (start + 1) % cap; }   // the oldest has been dropped
else          { ++n; }
```

Exactly one of the two numbers moves on every write: `n` while there is room, `start` once there is not. That is the whole invariant of a ring buffer with overwrite, and it is worth saying out loud because it is the thing the broken version half-knew.

### Why it looked fine at first

The failure needs `cap + 1` writes before it can show, and even then the count and the set of values stay correct — only the order is wrong. A test that writes fewer values than the capacity passes. A test that checks `count` passes. A test that sorts the output before comparing passes. This is the ordinary shape of an off-by-one in a wrapping index: correct until it wraps, and then wrong in a way that still looks plausible.

### Other ways to fix it

Any implementation meeting the specification is accepted. Two common alternatives:

- **Keep `start` and `end` and a `full` flag.** Writing advances `end`; if the buffer was full it advances `start` too. The flag exists because `start == end` is ambiguous between empty and full.
- **Keep a monotonically increasing write counter** `w`, and compute everything from it: the number held is `min(w, cap)`, and the oldest sits at `w <= cap ? 0 : w % cap`. No special case on write at all, which is why some people prefer it.
